item.title: US, Iran weigh mediators' latest proposals amid limited airstrikes
item.description: Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and a senior negotiator with the US, said his country had “delivered a strong and rational response to the American side,” according to a report ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Fiona MacDonald and Ahmed Elimam Iran  and the US are reviewing the latest proposals from mediators on how to bridge their divides and avert another round of all-out war, according to a diplomat briefed on the matter. Qatari mediators flew to Tehran on Monday for more talks with Iranian officials and returned late in the day, said the diplomat, who asked not to be named discussing sensitive matters. The talks in the Iranian capital were positive, the diplomat said. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and a senior negotiator with the US, said his country had “delivered a strong and rational response to the American side,” according to a report from Iran’s Fars news agency. “The ball is now in America’s court to prevent a war,” he added, reiterating Iran is ready to retaliate fiercely against any US-Israeli attacks. The latest diplomatic efforts follow weeks of heightened tensions, with Iran stepping up strikes on ships around the Strait of Hormuz and US President Donald Trump signaling he could order a new bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic after Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which his Republican party is expected to lose many seats in Congress to the Democrats. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has in recent weeks talked up the need for regime change in Iran. Axios reported on Sunday that he is pressing Trump to strike Iran right after the vote. The US overnight struck targets on the Iranian island of Qeshm inside the strait, according to several American media outlets.  They were limited military actions, designed to help ships sail safely through the waterway, and, at least in once instance, were in response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps firing at an American jet, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing unidentified US officials. The US has not announced the attacks. While oil prices have soared over the past month on worsening tensions — further hurting Trump’s political standing among Americans — they tumbled around 10% on Monday on signs the White House is willing to allow more time for a diplomatic resolution. Brent crude rose 1.7% to $106.50 a barrel in early trading on Tuesday, but remains far below last week’s close of almost $118. “They want to make a deal, and that could happen,” Trump told reporters in Washington during his closing message before the midterm elections. He added that oil prices had fallen because “it looks like that’s coming together very nicely.” When a reporter shouted a question about whether he would resume military strikes after the elections, Trump mouthed: “No.” Earlier on Monday, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government has been granted more authority by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to pursue peace talks. “We are striving to resolve the issue through dialogue and, in this regard, the supreme leader has also granted certain powers to the government,” the state-run Islamic Republic News Agency cited Pezeshkian as saying. The Iranian president didn’t clarify the extent of the new authority bestowed by Khamenei or whether it signals a broader shift for the Islamic Republic. Trump has repeatedly said he will resolve the Iran conflict soon, either with a deal or by resuming extensive strikes. The war began in late February when the US and Israel started bombing Iranian targets and assassinating senior officials in strikes, including former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. US officials initially talked of a war lasting no more than four to six weeks and Trump has grown frustrated with Iran’s resilience. It caused chaos across the Persian Gulf region with counter-strikes on American allies such as the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. And it effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz for a period by attacking ships, boosting oil and liquefied natural gas prices. The rise in fuel costs, with diesel hitting a record in the US and gasoline surpassing $4 a gallon on average, contributed to Americans turning against the conflict. Following a truce in early April, the sides have skirmished regularly, though with far less intensity than during the first phase of the war. They agreed on a so-called memorandum on understanding in June that was meant to lead to a formal peace, but it broke down within about two weeks. After his remarks on Monday, Trump wrote on social media that “Oil Prices are DROPPING LIKE A ROCK, down almost $10 a Barrel, A RECORD, because people feel that there will not be a War with Iran.” Trump’s Vice President JD Vance echoed the more dovish comments on Monday.  “We’ve had a number of good conversations with the Iranians,” he told reporters. “The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. Of course, the Iranians are always a little unpredictable.” Major differences seem to remain between the warring sides. Tehran wants a US naval blockade of its ports lifted and US pledges to ease sanctions and release frozen assets. Washington is demanding concessions related to Iran’s nuclear program. “Consultations and deliberations have become highly intensive,” Iran Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said during a visit to Turkmenistan. “We have presented our terms and plan, and everything depends on Washington’s political rationality. If they intend deception and military operations, they will face a response harsher and heavier than before.” Key to Iran’s strategy is getting a deal that ensures there’ll be no future attacks by the US or Israel, according to Ali Vaez, director of the Iran Project at the International Crisis Group. “Tehran is willing to negotiate an end to the war, but it wants more than a pause before the next round of hostilities,” he said. “It seeks a durable peace that restores its deterrence.” Khamenei has ordered his top military commanders to prepare for renewed confrontation with the US and Israel and expand Tehran’s options for retaliation. That has fueled fears among Gulf Arab states that a better-prepared Iran could unleash an even more destructive war across the region, leaving them to pick up the pieces.

item.title: India tax hike drives illegal gold imports to highest level since 2023
item.description: Informal shipments for July to September jumped more than 1,500% to 50 metric tons from 3 tons a year earlier, according to a report from the World Gold Council ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Yihui Xie and Preeti Soni India’s illegal gold imports surged to the highest since 2023 in the third quarter as a government duty hike spurred use of unofficial channels, according to a report from the World Gold Council.  Informal shipments for July to September jumped more than 1,500% to 50 metric tons from 3 tons a year earlier, the producer-funded group said, citing data from consultancy Metals Focus. The report gave no details on how the trade is tracked. Such imports typically go through avenues that avoid official duties, like smuggling or small quantities brought in by individuals. In the past, tax hikes have tended to “increase the incentive” for inflows through such channels, WGC added.  The informal bullion market in the world’s second-largest consumer has flourished since the government more than doubled import levies on gold and silver to 15% earlier this year. The move was as part of efforts to curb purchases as India tackles a ballooning trade deficit due to higher energy prices.  Indians buy the precious metal to celebrate births, religious festivals and, above all, weddings. It can serve as adornment, gift or contribution to family savings. Since there’s little domestic production, most demand is met through imports, which weighs heavily on the trade bill and the currency. The move to raise taxes has also prompted more Indian households to turn to under-the-counter cash sales, where bullion and jewelry change hands without invoices that can be traced by authorities.  The country’s gold demand — spanning jewelry and investments — increased from the previous quarter, but most metrics point to a decline from a year earlier. Consumption typically increases in the last quarter, with major festivals like Diwali set to encourage purchases, the report said.  However, there are signs the expected increase may not come through. Jewelers are holding back for now, according to the country’s biggest precious metal refiner, as they bet that a recent drop in prices has further to run. Gold slumped 6.8% in October and broke under the key price of $4,000 an ounce, and has traded below that level since.

item.description: The appointment comes as OpenAI steps up its work with defence agencies and governments on AI applications in national security and cybersecurity ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Technology / Tech News / Why OpenAI has hired ex-US Army secretary Dan Driscoll for 'security' role

Why OpenAI has hired ex-US Army secretary Dan Driscoll for 'security' role The appointment comes as OpenAI steps up its work with defence agencies and governments on AI applications in national security and cybersecurity

The appointment also builds on OpenAI's Daybreak programme, through which the company is working with allies and partners to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services | Image Credit: Bloomberg

Apexa Rai New Delhi 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 03 2026 | 10:27 AM IST

Listen to This Article

OpenAI has brought in a former secretary of the US Army to help it figure out how to put artificial intelligence to work in national security, from improving military operations to strengthening cyber defences.   The company on Monday announced the appointment of Dan Driscoll, who served as the 26th Secretary of the US Army, as its senior counsellor for national security modernisation. The newly created role will involve advising OpenAI's leadership and its public- and private-sector partners on how advanced AI can be used to strengthen national and cybersecurity.   In its announcement, OpenAI said Driscoll would work with governments, industry, academic institutions and US allies to identify practical ways of using AI in national security. He will also help the company's teams understand the operational requirements of security institutions around the world.

Who is Dan Driscoll? Driscoll previously served as the 26th Secretary of the US Army, overseeing its operations, modernisation and resources. His responsibilities covered nearly one million active-duty, National Guard and Reserve soldiers, as well as more than 265,000 Army civilian employees, according to OpenAI.   During his tenure, he worked on accelerating the adoption of new technology, reforming military procurement and modernising the Army. He has also served as acting director of the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF). Why has OpenAI hired a former Army secretary? Driscoll's experience in the military and government is expected to help OpenAI understand what defence institutions need from AI tools and how these can be put to practical use.

In its announcement, the company said he would advise public- and private-sector partners on changes to policy and strategy that could help unlock AI applications in national security. His role will also involve identifying areas where military requirements, institutional changes and emerging AI capabilities intersect.   Driscoll said military personnel needed better tools to keep pace with rapidly changing national security requirements.   "The people who serve deserve the very best tools we can put in their hands," he said, adding that AI could help them cut through paperwork, make sense of larger volumes of information and get the right answers to the right people faster.

He said he was joining OpenAI to help the US and its allies use the technology responsibly.   OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the US had an opportunity to work with other countries to expand the adoption of what he described as "democratic AI" and strengthen American leadership. What is OpenAI's Daybreak programme? The appointment also builds on OpenAI's Daybreak programme, through which the company is working with allies and partners to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services.   The initiative focuses on helping organisations identify and address software vulnerabilities before they can be exploited. This is particularly relevant for critical infrastructure and institutions that may face cyber threats.

OpenAI's work in this area has included supporting cyber-defence efforts in European countries, including France, Germany and Poland. It has also provided Ukraine access to tools to help identify software vulnerabilities, according to the Financial Times . OpenAI's growing defence ambitions The hiring comes as OpenAI expands its relationship with the US government and defence establishment.   Earlier this year, the company agreed to deploy its AI models in classified settings for the US Department of Defence. The development followed the collapse of negotiations between the Pentagon and rival AI company Anthropic over the terms governing military use of its technology.   The use of AI in defence has raised questions about how the technology can be deployed safely, particularly in sensitive military and intelligence operations. While AI can help process information and identify security threats, its use also requires safeguards and human oversight.

item.title: US FDA grants tentative nod to Dr Reddy's twice-yearly HIV prevention drug
item.description: The tentative approval for generic lenacapavir is expected to accelerate affordable access to the twice-yearly HIV prevention injection across 120 countries outside the US.
item.dc:creator: Anjali Singh
item.content:encoded: Dr Reddy’s Laboratories has received tentative approval from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its generic version of lenacapavir, a long-acting injectable drug administered twice a year to prevent HIV infection. The approval is expected to accelerate access to the drug across 120 countries outside the US under a voluntary licensing agreement with its innovator, Gilead Sciences. The approval has been granted under the FDA’s President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) programme. Under an existing agreement with Unitaid, the Wits Reproductive Health and HIV Institute (Wits RHI) and the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI), the injectable is expected to be made available at $40 per person annually across the 120 countries covered by Gilead’s voluntary licence. The first supplies are expected to reach countries before the end of 2026, with a broader rollout across eligible markets in 2027, the company said on Monday. The development follows a voluntary licence granted by Gilead to Dr Reddy’s in October 2024. In September 2025, the Hyderabad-based drugmaker entered into an agreement with Unitaid, Wits RHI and CHAI to support product development, expedite regulatory approvals and facilitate affordable access to the drug. Lenacapavir offers an alternative to existing pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) options, which often require more frequent administration. Given twice a year, the long-acting injectable is intended to reduce the risk of sexually acquired HIV-1 in adults and adolescents weighing at least 35 kg. “This is a moment of immense pride for all of us at Dr Reddy’s. Developing and manufacturing a complex long-acting injectable like lenacapavir at an affordable price required strong scientific capabilities and manufacturing expertise to address an urgent access need,” said Deepak Sapra, chief executive officer, API and Services, Dr Reddy’s Laboratories. The FDA's tentative approval marks a significant regulatory milestone, although wider availability will also depend on further steps, including World Health Organization (WHO) prequalification and national regulatory approvals in individual markets. The approval comes amid efforts to expand access to long-acting HIV prevention options, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, where daily medication can pose challenges to adherence and uptake. Unitaid said its support had helped accelerate the timeline for generic lenacapavir, bringing the approval process closer to the originator's launch rather than the decade-long gap often seen in generic drug development. “Now, with lenacapavir, we have helped shorten that timeline to just over a year. For young women in Africa, this translates into faster access to a groundbreaking HIV prevention option,” said Philippe Duneton, executive director of Unitaid. The WHO has also recommended twice-yearly lenacapavir in its HIV prevention guidelines. However, health systems will need to prepare for its introduction through provider training, community engagement and wider delivery infrastructure, Wits RHI said. Dr Reddy’s said the development strengthens its public health access portfolio and demonstrates its capabilities in developing and manufacturing complex medicines. The company is working with its partners to support product introduction and generate real-world evidence to guide its rollout across underserved populations.
